newsitem.title: UK: UK Jan PMI rises to 54.0, pace of growth picks up.
newsitem.headline: UK Jan PMI rises to 54.0, pace of growth picks up.

text.p: Britain's Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) rose to a seasonally-adjusted 54.0 percent in January from 52.8 in December, the first rise in the pace of manufacturing growth since last October, the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said.
The figure signalled growth in the manufacturing sector for the eighth month in a row, with rising domestic demand prompting an increase in the rate of growth of new orders.
"The improvement in the PMI was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders," the CIPS said.
It said the absence of capacity constraints was linked to weak world-wide demand for many key raw materials, which also led to a softening of prices paid for inputs.
"However, by far the most significant factor affecting input prices was the exchange rate," the CIPS said.
It said sterling's appreciation had led to a sharp fall in import prices, which had resulted in the sharpest drop in purchase prices since last August.
Stocks of purchases fell sharply in January on good availability of cheap supplies.
There was also a further fall in finished goods stock due to deliberate de-stocking policies.
"The fall in these stocks was not as marked as in December, however, due to a greater incidence of stock building in preparation for anticipated stronger demand in coming months," the CIPS said.
It said employment also rose in January, the largest increase for nearly two years. It was the sixth consecutive monthly rise.
Following is a table of seasonally adjusted PMI indices (previously reported December figures in brackets):
JANUARY DECEMBER
Purchasing Managers' Index 54.0 52.8 (52.5)
Quantity of Purchases 52.7 50.0 (49.7)
Suppliers' Delivery Times 48.2 47.7 (47.7)
Stocks of Purchases 45.6 41.8 (41.6)
Stocks of Finished Goods 46.1 44.3 (44.4)
Employment 53.1 51.7 (51.2)

NOTE: The PMI is based on a weighted average of seasonally adjusted measures of output, new orders, suppliers' delivery times, stocks of items purchased and employment. A reading above 50 indicates that manufacturing is generally expanding, below 50 that it is generally declining.
-- Jennifer Scott, London newsroom +44 171 542 7708
